title: Language models use information best at the start or end of long contexts
source_title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
quote: highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle
summary: Multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval show accuracy peaking when relevant text is at the beginning or end of the input, with significant degradation when it sits in the middle, including for explicitly long-context models.

title: Removing literal needle-haystack overlap exposes long-context retrieval decay
source_title: NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching
quote: performance degrades significantly as context length increases. At 32K, for instance, 11 models drop below 50% of their strong short-length baselines.
summary: Introduces NoLiMa, a needle-in-a-haystack benchmark where needle and haystack share little wording, forcing latent association; models that claim 128K+ contexts degrade sharply as context grows, pointing to attention difficulty over long distances.

title: Spacing between multiple relevant passages creates positional bias in long contexts
source_title: Distance between Relevant Information Pieces Causes Bias in Long-Context LLMs
quote: These experiments reveal that while most current models are robust against the "lost in the middle" issue, there exist significant biases related to the spacing of relevant information pieces.
summary: LongPiBench tests long contexts containing multiple relevant information pieces; while most tested models avoid the classic middle-position drop, significant bias appears based on how far apart the relevant pieces are spaced.

title: Lost-in-the-middle weakens beyond half the context window, shifting to distance bias
source_title: Positional Biases Shift as Inputs Approach Context Window Limits
quote: the LiM effect is strongest when inputs occupy up to 50% of a model's context window. Beyond that, the primacy bias weakens, while recency bias remains relatively stable.
summary: Measures input length relative to each model's own context window: the lost-in-the-middle effect is strongest below half the window, then primacy bias weakens and a distance-to-end bias dominates; retrieval appears to be a prerequisite for reasoning.

title: Lost-in-the-middle traced to pre-training retrieval demands, not simple information loss
source_title: Lost in the Middle: An Emergent Property from Information Retrieval Demands in LLMs
quote: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) often degrades when crucial information is in the middle of a long context
summary: Trains small models from scratch on human-memory-like retrieval demands and finds the U-shaped middle-position curve emerges from those demands plus autoregressive properties and attention sinks, rather than from information loss alone.

title: HN post warns against trusting large context windows in practice
summary: Hacker News discussion of a blog post whose title warns against trusting large context windows; 277 points and 195 comments indicate substantial community attention on long-context reliability.

title: Report on context rot examines how growing input token counts affect LLM performance
source_title: Context Rot: How increasing input tokens impacts LLM performance
summary: Hacker News discussion of a technical report titled 'Context Rot: How increasing input tokens impacts LLM performance'; 260 points and 59 comments indicate strong attention to input-length effects on model performance.

title: Benchmark evaluates coding LLMs at context windows up to one million tokens
source_title: LongCodeBench: Evaluating Coding LLMs at 1M Context Windows
summary: Hacker News submission of 'LongCodeBench: Evaluating Coding LLMs at 1M Context Windows', linking to an arXiv benchmark for coding evaluation at very long contexts; relevant to whether long-context retrieval holds for code tasks (small thread, 25 points).

title: Explainer argues LLMs forget information placed in the middle of their input
source_title: Lost in the Middle: Why LLMs Forget What They Just Read
summary: Hacker News submission of a Substack explainer titled 'Lost in the Middle: Why LLMs Forget What They Just Read', on middle-context recall failure; the thread is small (4 points).

title: Paper links attention patterns to context-rot degradation in retrieval
source_title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval
summary: Hacker News submission of a paper whose title claims attention predicts context rot in long-context retrieval, giving a mechanism-level account of degradation; the thread is small (3 points).
